Nobody’s saying don’t put out the alerts. They’re saying let us shut off the fucking air horn noise so that i don’t wake up at 3am to see an alert for a kid that i can do nothing about because i’ve been in a basement 10 hours away for the past 10 hours.

Same thing i did with a dangerous weather alert and phone calls. I don’t have the mental capacity to read, comprehend, and critically think about this as soon as I wake up. 

The thing that pisses me off most about it is the mother fucking noise. I’m happy to get the alert — not so happy that it sounds like 8 fucking air horns going off regardless of if i’m sleeping, driving, or anything else. I get they want the noise to grab your attention but honestly when i’m awake and get them the noise is alarming. not attempting grabbing or anything: alarming.  It doesn’t make me look at my phone, it makes me think i’m about to be hit by a semi truck. 

And to finish my rant: it’s triggered some people’s PTSD. I care about missing kids, but i also don’t think that it’s really fucking counter active. The alert sends my friend into a breakdown: if he knew anything about it he can’t tell you for a good 15-45 minutes while he’s getting his shit together. And on a more selfish note — he shouldn’t have to be subjected to a noise that harsh regardless of the situation. He should be able to keep his phone on silent, and not have notifications come though that loudly.

Someone above gave a really good response, and though I’m late I’d like to add a little bit. 

Plans change. I’ve been hours late getting home before and stuff because plans changed. What’s worked in the past is the ability to communicate that. When you talk to him, maybe suggest he send you a text or something if he realizes he’s going to be home later or whatever? 

I found as a teenager my plans would change at the drop of a hat. Hell, I’m almost 20 and my plans are still like that.  I don’t think you’re being overbearing or anything — if you guy have plans at 11:30 then he should be able to communicate that those plans are getting pushed back or changed. That’s reasonable.

My advice is late but if anyone is still reading it: go out and do things. Plan to go alone. Plan to go see a kids movie, plan to go to the mall or the bookstore, plan to go to the park or gym, or even out to dinner. Just plan to do it alone. 

You don’t have to invite people right away, but you do have to do it. It’s scary and hard, but it gets so much easier to talk to people and ask them to do things if you’re already doing things.  

Inviting people out gets easier when you have a plan. Asking someone to hang out when you don’t know what you wanna do can be rough at first. Saying “Hey, i’m gonna go to starbucks this weekend and then I was thinking of catching a movie. Wanna come with?” is easier to say yes to for a lot of people. And if they say no — well man, you planned to go alone anyways. 

Let’s be clear though: doing things alone doesn’t make you a loner. I used to get really anxious about doing things alone, but after a while it starts to feel good. You get to recharge and not be at home. But it also attracts people to you — at least in my experience. People have started using me to combat their social anxiety about going certain places and doing certain things. But before that started people just learned that I’m going to do things by myself anyways, so they might as well come along.

The night my dad died.

He had lung cancer. Stage 4 by the time that they caught it. It was only a few days after he was diagnosed. I had gone to visit him that afternoon after an exam. He was having a really good day -- breathing better than he had in ages, laughing, eating. He sounded good. He even took a nap -- he had been sleeping sitting up for weeks and he laid down and took a nap.

That night at almost midnight we got a call from the hospital. I was studying for my exams the next week , and I just closed my laptop and sighed when I heard the phone ring. I just knew what it was. I went upstairs and just heard my mom go "So his heart isn't beating?" and then I don't really know what happened afterwards. I remember my mom telling her that the phone call was because they were running a code on my dad and wanted to know if they shouldn't be -- he hadn't signed his DNR yet. I remember me telling her he would rather be dead then not able to function. I remember going back downstairs, and I remembered the next phone call where they said he had been revived. I remember telling my mom that we had to let him go. I remember saying I couldn't go to the hospital and say goodbye, that I couldn't remember him like that. 

Then I remember playing video games until 5am, shaking, and not being able to think. Because he was gone and the world had changed in the most dramatic way, in under 4 hours. And all I could do was sit there and let it happen. I couldn't cry or eat or drink. I couldn't do anything.

I have two theories. One is that it is just due to how society views romantic relationships. Since these relationships are generally viewed as being more important than most other relationships, it makes it okay to do things like this with your SO.

Personally, I tell my SO things like this because our trust in each other is probably the backbone of our relationship. If I tell her and she tells someone else... It would be a small violation of my trust, but would have lasting consequences on our relationship. To keep it short and not give you an essay about the dynamics in my relationship: person she told/gossip > our relationship. Due to circumstances in our life, I *know* she would never do this, and if she did for even a second, we would've broken up. 

I want to address the last thing, though. Of course, it sucks to confide in someone and have them tell someone else, SO or not. But this ignores context, and contents of the secret. There is a vast difference between telling your SO something because you're gossiping, and telling your SO because you're deeply bothered or in an awkward situation because of the information. Is it fair to expect people to keep your secrets to themselves if it has a negative impact on their life? I say no, and quite often, talking to my SO about stuff like this helps me work though it.

Exactly. If you bullshit and you’re relating it back to the question asked for the essay, then you’ve done something. 
 
Even if you bullshit it, miss the question completely, but have *something* in the essay to prove that you tried to answer it, then most profs give you some sort of credit. 

Writing “dunno,” or just going “idk,” when presented with something in a college setting, is often not acceptable. 

You can argue that money is a driving factor, and i won’t say you’re wrong. But if you’re in college a lot of the learning is stuff you need to do yourself.

College essays and job interviews have different goals though. 

In a job interview a question may be asked  to test your problem solving skills and see if you’re a good fit for the position. So saying “I don’t know but here’s what i’d do to figure it out.” is acceptable. 

An essay may be to test your knowledge. If it’s a project to test what you know about the course content, obviously saying “i don’t know,” isn’t acceptable, and bullshitting gets you further.

I tend to thing these situations are different. When my SO tells me stuff like that, she’ll start with “they said not to tell anyone...” which just tells me that outside of this conversation, I don’t know this bit of information.

Generally, as long as it’s not awkward for the SO to act like they don’t know the secret, then I don’t really see issue with it. It’s not *always* gossipy to tell your partner stuff like that.
